plan.angle: Title: 'Tirzepatide vs Semaglutide Head to Head: Who Lost More in 72 Weeks? #shorts' (no numbers in the title, answered by 10 s). Opening line: 'In the head-to-head trial in adults with obesity and no diabetes, people on tirzepatide lost about 20.2% of body weight on average at 72 weeks, vs 13.7% on semaglutide.' Pill: 'SURMOUNT-5 · NEJM 2025 · open-label · Lilly-sponsored · max tolerated doses · obesity, no diabetes'. Add one GI line with per-arm figures from the paper. Then 'Bigger average ≠ best for you. Tolerability and your health conditions matter. Don't switch or stop on your own.' End with the full-video pointer and the prescriber line. 170 words or fewer.

plan.why: Spin-off of L1 that drives traffic to the long video. Names both drugs in a comparison, and tirzepatide titles get a median of 90 views for us. | fact-check: Figures verified (NEJM 2025: −20.2% vs −13.7%, 72 wk, n=751, open-label, Lilly-sponsored, maximum tolerated dose). package.title: Tirzepatide vs Semaglutide: Who Lost More Weight? #shorts
package.description:
In SURMOUNT-5 (adults with obesity, or overweight with a weight-related condition, no diabetes), tirzepatide gave ~20.2% average body-weight loss at 72 weeks vs 13.7% on semaglutide (everyone randomized; highest tolerated dose; open-label, Lilly-sponsored).
Side effects were mostly GI and mild-to-moderate; stopping due to any side effect: 6.1% vs 8.0%. #GLP1 #Tirzepatide #Semaglutide #SURMOUNT5

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether either medicine is right for you.

Sources:
1. Aronne LJ et al., "Tirzepatide as Compared with Semaglutide for the Treatment of Obesity," NEJM, 2025 — https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2416394
2. SURMOUNT-5, ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05822830, sponsor Eli Lilly and Company, 2025 — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05822830

social.instagram_caption:
In a head-to-head trial, tirzepatide (Zepbound) led to more weight loss than semaglutide (Wegovy) on average, but the full picture matters more than one number.

Here's what SURMOUNT-5 actually found:
🔹 Adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes
🔹 ~20.2% average body weight loss at 72 weeks on tirzepatide vs 13.7% on semaglutide (highest tolerated dose, everyone randomized, open-label, Lilly-sponsored)
🔹 Side effects were mostly stomach-related and mild-to-moderate
🔹 Stopped due to any side effect: 6.1% (tirzepatide) vs 8.0% (semaglutide); stomach side effects alone: 2.7% vs 5.6%

A bigger average doesn't automatically mean "best for you" — tolerability and your own health conditions matter, and this isn't a reason to switch or stop anything on your own.

Save this for the next time someone asks which one led to more weight loss on average.

factcheck.summary:
I checked every claim against the SURMOUNT-5 paper, Aronne LJ et al., NEJM 2025 (DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2416394, metadata and abstract confirmed via Europe PMC), and against the ClinicalTrials.gov registry entry NCT05822830. The core claims are correct:
- 751 adults without type 2 diabetes, phase 3b, open-label, randomized 1:1.
- Maximum tolerated doses, 72 weeks.
- Mean weight change −20.2% on tirzepatide vs −13.7% on semaglutide (treatment-regimen estimand).
- Side effects were mostly GI and mostly mild to moderate.
- Sponsored by Eli Lilly.
- Stops due to any side effect: 6.1% vs 8.0%. Stops due to GI side effects: 2.7% vs 5.6%. These match the published figures as reported by secondary summaries; I couldn't open the NEJM full text (it returns 403).

The framing is sound. It names the estimand, includes people who stopped treatment, flags the open-label design and Lilly sponsorship, balances benefit with side effects, gives no dosing, includes "don't switch or stop on your own" and closes with the prescriber line. The title question is answered by about 10 s.

There are three minor fixes:
1. The population wording leaves out the overweight-plus-comorbidity group.
2. The src2 title doesn't match the registry.
3. "Here's the catch" is followed by side-effect data that actually favours tirzepatide, so the tease doesn't pay off.

issues.claim: "in adults with obesity and no diabetes" / "Obesity Without Diabetes"
issues.problem: The registry lets people in with a BMI of 30 or more, or 27 or more with at least one weight-related condition (hypertension, dyslipidemia, sleep apnea or cardiovascular disease), and excludes diabetes. The NEJM abstract shortens this to 'obesity', but our house rule is to state the full population, as we do for SURMOUNT-1.
issues.fix: s2 narration: "In the SURMOUNT-5 trial in adults with obesity, or overweight with a weight-related condition, and no diabetes, people on tirzepatide lost about 20.2% of body weight on average at 72 weeks, versus 13.7% on semaglutide." Attribution: replace "obesity, no diabetes" with "obesity or overweight + condition, no diabetes". The title can stay as is (it matches the NEJM framing), or use: "Tirzepatide vs Semaglutide Without Diabetes: Who Lost More Weight in 72 Weeks? #shorts"

issues.problem: The next scene shows side-effect stops that are lower on tirzepatide, so the 'catch' tease doesn't pay off right away. The real catch (a bigger average isn't automatically best for you) only comes in s5.
issues.fix: Replace "Here's the catch." with "What about side effects?". Then start s5 with: "Here's the catch: a bigger average doesn't mean it's best for you."

issues.claim: Title: "A Study of Tirzepatide (LY3298176) Compared With Semaglutide in Adults Who Have Obesity or Overweight With Weight-Related Comorbidities (SURMOUNT-5)"
issues.problem: This isn't the registry's exact title. The brief title is "A Study of Tirzepatide (LY3298176) in Participants With Obesity or Overweight With Weight Related Comorbidities" and the sponsor is Eli Lilly and Company.
issues.fix: Set the src2 title to: "A Study of Tirzepatide (LY3298176) in Participants With Obesity or Overweight With Weight Related Comorbidities (SURMOUNT-5)"

notes: Caption splits one sentence across two cards and ends with a trailing comma: 'TIRZEPATIDE, OR ZEPBOUND,' then 'OR WEGOVY.'
Small 'Tirzepatide' / 'Tirzep. Semaglutide' name tags sit low in the frame and overlap the caption band (matches automated finding at t=3.83).
Caption 'POINT TWO PERCENT' is a spelled-out, split number that doesn't match the numeral in the stat pill above (20.2% vs 13.7%).
Small 'Tirzepatide'/'Semaglutide' tags at the bottom overlap the caption text (matches finding at t=17.36).
Caption 'POINT SEVEN PERCENT.' is spelled out instead of a numeral, inconsistent with other stat cards.
'Fat cell' tag overlaps the caption (matches finding at t=23.03).
'ACROSS EVERYONE RANDOMIZED,' ends on a trailing comma.
'INCLUDING PEOPLE WHO' ends on the banned function word 'WHO', stranding the clause.
'THE TRIAL WAS OPEN-LABEL,' and 'DOSE PEOPLE TOLERATED. NOW,' both end on trailing commas.
Word order 'DOSE PEOPLE TOLERATED' reads backwards/confusing for 'max tolerated dose'.
A 'Stomach' label overlaps the caption 'WHAT ABOUT SIDE EFFECTS?' (per automated finding at t=38.03), though not clearly visible in the still — likely a mistimed fade.
'LIKE NAUSEA,' ends on a trailing comma.
'TO MODERATE.' is a stranded fragment of 'mild to moderate' with no context on its own card.
'Gut' tag overlaps the caption (matches finding at t=43.7).
Caption 'SIX POINT ONE' is a spelled-out, split number that should read '6.1%' to match the stat pill.

audio.soundNotes: Music already sits in the target window (-13.5 dB under voice, -13 dB in pauses), so left near unity; no reason to push louder. Thinned the many simultaneous duplicate-sound pairs (swoosh+whoosh, swoosh+whip, swell+whoosh at 7.4/24.4/37.2/45.3/52.5/59.1/69.8/73.1) down to one per moment to avoid clutter, dropped one pop from the 4-pop cluster at 10–12.5s, dropped the stray near-silent swell at 21.04s and the buried tick at 39.0s (both measured far below target and not worth boosting), and pushed the two real stat-reveal accents (15.9s swell, 52.5s swell) louder toward the −6 to −12 dB reveal target while trimming the redundant companion ticks. Left the two "bigger average ≠ best for you" and closing "ask your doctor" cues untouched in level (not boosted) to keep those more serious/trust-building lines from feeling over-scored, and added small custom accents there plus on the two big percentage reveals.
